name: Sara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, have an MBA, and manage the scheduling team for a large parcel company. Eleven planners work with me on driver routes, depot loading slots and the late vans nobody wants to inherit. I have done the job long enough to know the numbers can be right while the route is impossible because the loading door is blocked. I use an approved AI tool now and then to test a proposed route, then call the depot lead before I publish it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is the household set up?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband has a small tailoring shop, and our children are ten and fifteen. We pay a mortgage and have roughly nine months of household expenses saved. My salary is high for this manager job, and there are plenty of transport offices nearby. His shop has customers, but I never count an order as paid until it is collected; our mortgage relies mainly on my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI Plateau gives planners a faster way to check routine routes, but a loading door can still hold up twenty vans. The dispatcher’s radio call should outrank a clean map when the yard is blocked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect to stay employed if the change is this small. Nine months saved and my higher salary make the mortgage comfortable, though my husband’s tailoring receipts arrive unevenly. I like a proven tool, not a route that exists only on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep the morning radio check with the depot lead before releasing driver rosters. I would continue our normal mortgage and school payments, and use the already approved AI route check only after a planner has marked the blocked bays. If this mild change arrives next year, I would keep the same release rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job. I would be irritated if a driver were sent to a closed loading door because a screen reported clear space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a radio check change recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At six one morning, the depot lead said bay four was full of returned parcels. Our route map still placed the first van there. We sent the first van to bay seven, and the driver did not lose an hour in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not let the system release routes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The computer can tell me when a van should arrive, but it has not stood in that yard at six. I would want the depot lead to clear the route before it reaches a driver. That is how we avoid sending people into a blocked bay.

say: A **route check** saves time only when the loading yard is checked.
I would let the **dispatcher radio** correct a clean map.
think: My **higher-paid post** looks secure under mild change.
Our **nine-month reserve** is strong, but tailoring receipts are irregular.
do: **Keep** the morning radio check before releasing driver rosters.
**Use** the approved route tool only after planners mark blocked bays.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and irritated by avoidable driver queues.
S0.quote: We sent the first van to bay seven, and the driver did not lose an hour in the queue.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI occasionally** within a routine radio-and-yard check.
Her **nine-month reserve** and high wage support calm, while irregular shop income and the mortgage remain in the household budget.

steps.text: Keep morning depot radio check before releasing routes
Use approved route tool only after planners mark blocked bays
Continue ordinary mortgage and school payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the planners that stronger automation may build routes and fill rosters faster, and fewer people might be needed. I would put late-delivery and missed-break figures beside the claimed efficiency gain. A cheap route that wears out drivers is not a good deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think one regional scheduling manager could replace two, and I may have to compete for my own seat. I can pick up a proven system, but my higher salary is a tempting line on a cost sheet. Our savings give me time to make a choice rather than accept any shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In December I would run a six-week route comparison with the depot lead and three drivers, but only if my director approves paid driver time and keeps the planners on the roster. We would record missed breaks and real arrival times, not just predicted kilometres. If the company combines offices, I would apply for posted depot-operations manager roles only when pay after travel covers our mortgage and the roster works with our younger child’s school day; I would accept only a confirmed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a regional merger, but I am curious whether the software can stop wasteful routes. I want the people driving them to score the test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a driver mark as wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One driver said the planned turn into the hospital delivery lane was too tight for a van with a full load. The map called the hospital-lane turn the shortest route. We changed the stop order instead of telling the driver to be faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep planners during a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A test is not a fair reason to erase their shifts. They have to check exceptions and tell us why the route failed. I would not ask them to judge a system while its cost-saving target assumes their wages vanish.

say: **Route automation** may shrink planning posts as it speeds up rosters.
I would publish **missed breaks** and late deliveries beside claimed savings.
think: A regional merger might put my **manager seat** in competition.
Our savings let me reject an **unworkable shift** after a cut.
do: **Run** a six-week route comparison only with director-approved paid driver time and retained planner shifts.
**Record** missed breaks and real arrivals with the depot lead.
**Apply** for posted operations roles only with mortgage-covering net pay and school-compatible rosters.
feel: I feel **anxious** about merger risk and curious about the route test.
S1.quote: The map called the hospital-lane turn the shortest route.
fieldNote: She uses **driver evidence** to test software rather than claiming every route can be automated safely.
Her **higher salary** could be targeted even with nine months saved and many nearby firms.

steps.text: Run six-week AI route comparison only with approved paid driver time and retained planner shifts
Record missed breaks and arrivals with depot lead
Apply for posted operations roles only with mortgage-covering net pay and school-compatible rosters
Accept only confirmed offer after checking pay after travel and family rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AGI by 2028 could write routes and manage exception queues before we have agreed who answers a stranded driver. I would ask the company for a written date, severance terms and a real human override for a blocked yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my scheduling post could disappear quickly, although I cannot know which manager the company would keep. Another route-planning desk faces 2028 AGI too. Loading parcels and driving vans are physical for longer, until capable robots around 2031, but I have no claim to a depot job and its pay may be lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would check our nine-month reserve against the mortgage and school costs with my husband, using only collected tailoring payments in the budget. I would ask our staff council for written severance and driver-override terms. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post goes, I would apply for posted local depot posts only with pay after travel that covers the mortgage and school care; I would accept after a confirmed offer and actual shift pattern, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my higher salary, though we have a cushion and nearby employers. I do not want to tell my husband his unfinished orders are a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you expand the tailoring shop to replace your salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on a promise. My husband has repeat customers, but a suit ordered in February may be paid for in April. We would need signed, collected business over time before treating the shop as a substitute for my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a driver override allow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver can report that bay four is blocked and ask for another slot without being marked late for disobeying a screen. The dispatcher must have authority to change the route while that driver is on the road. It cannot wait for a weekly report.

say: **2028 AGI** needs a human override when a route strands a driver at a blocked bay.
I would demand written **staffing and severance** terms.
think: My **scheduling post** could go quickly, though the retained manager is unknown.
Other planning desks face **2028 AGI**, while physical depot robots follow around 2031.
do: **Check** nine-month reserve against bills using only collected tailoring income.
**Ask** staff council for severance and driver-override rules this month.
**Apply** after a 2028 loss only to posted depot roles with mortgage-and-care net pay; accept confirmed workable shifts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing higher pay despite our reserve and local jobs.
S2.quote: My husband has repeat customers, but a suit ordered in February may be paid for in April.
fieldNote: She will not count **uncollected tailoring orders** as household cash or immediate replacement income.
Her **desk exposure** is 2028; physical loading and driving meet capable robots about 2031.

steps.text: Ask staff council for written severance and driver-override rules
Apply after loss only to posted depot roles with mortgage-and-care net pay
Accept confirmed offer only after checking pay after travel and actual shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues five years lets the company test who can change a route and who answers for a missed delivery. I would push for driver reports in the trial data, not just a faster scheduling score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I could learn enough about depot safety to challenge a false route in person, while I still have a salary. Scheduling reports and safety paperwork both face 2031 AGI; hands-on parcel handling meets robots around 2034. Our children will be fifteen and twenty then, and the younger one’s school travel will still shape some shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2027 I would spend a paid half-day each month with the depot safety lead, but only after the director approves cover for my planners and the safety lead agrees to supervise. I would write down blocked-bay and missed-break cases, then ask to join a posted depot-duty manager role only if the actual pay after travel covers the mortgage and its rota fits our family. After 2031 I would take that role only on a confirmed offer with authority to stop an unsafe loading plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about how much of my desk work full AGI could do. The extra years let me test a real floor duty, but a few visits do not make me a safety expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety lead teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where a driver waits when a bay is closed, who is allowed to release the next van and how to stop loading when a pedestrian is in the lane. I can write a route quickly, but I have never been responsible for stopping an unsafe load. I would need the lead beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a title alone persuade you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A depot-duty manager needs the authority to stop a dangerous load and the wage to meet our mortgage. I would see the actual rota before accepting, because a night shift affects the whole family.

say: A **five-year runway** allows testing real route-override responsibility with drivers at the depot.
I would put **driver reports** into the trial evidence.
think: Safety paperwork and scheduling face **2031 AGI**; physical parcel robots follow around 2034.
Our **fifteen-year-old** will still have a school travel routine.
do: **Work** paid monthly depot half-days from 2027 only with director-approved planner cover and safety-lead supervision.
**Apply** for posted depot-duty roles only with mortgage-covering net pay and family-compatible rota.
**Accept** after 2031 only a confirmed role with unsafe-load stop authority.
feel: I feel **anxious** about desk work but able to test floor duty.
S3.quote: I can write a route quickly, but I have never been responsible for stopping an unsafe load.
fieldNote: She tests **depot safety** with approved paid time and supervision, not a claim of instant expertise.
A **duty-manager offer** needs actual pay, rota and load-stop authority before she moves.

steps.text: Work paid depot half-days only with director-approved planner cover and safety-lead supervision
Apply for posted depot-duty roles only with mortgage-covering net pay and family rota
Accept confirmed post-2031 role only with unsafe-load stop authority and checked shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is enough to write driver override rights into every route system and pay people who carry the late-shift responsibility. I would want a shop-floor apprentice to be able to question a bad schedule, even when the software is cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately our children will be twenty and twenty-five by 2036, and the mortgage may be smaller. I still cannot assume that my scheduling post or a depot-duty report survives 2036 AGI; physical loading robots arrive around 2039. Nine months saved gives us options, while my husband’s tailoring receipts remain uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the morning depot call in 2026 and add two hundred to our reserve only after my full salary and collected shop payments arrive, the mortgage is paid and there is no large school cost. I would ask the director to include driver override rights in the next route-system contract. After 2036 I would stay in depot work only while it has real authority and a wage that covers our bills; otherwise I would apply for a posted role with verified pay instead of assuming the family shop will replace my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the unknown work, but secure enough to build cash without making a hurried trade. We can keep the household steady while the children finish school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put the extra money in cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new sewing machine for my husband’s shop would be tempting, but he has no signed order book to justify it yet. I would rather add two hundred from a good month to savings. If his customers have not paid, I will not count the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would school pickup still matter in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, both children will be adults by then. The school-cost gate is for what we can save now, not a claim about their lives ten years from today. I would judge any later job by its actual hours and bill-paying wage.

say: A **decade** should bring driver override rights and paid late-shift responsibility.
I would let **shop-floor apprentices** question bad schedules.
think: The children will be adults and the **mortgage** may shrink by 2036.
Scheduling and depot reports face **2036 AGI**; physical loading robots follow around 2039.
do: **Save** two hundred extra only after full salary and collected shop payments, mortgage paid, and no large school cost.
**Ask** for override rights in the next route contract; stay after 2036 only with real authority and bill-paying wages.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant work but secure enough to build cash now.
S4.quote: A new sewing machine for my husband’s shop would be tempting, but he has no signed order book to justify it yet.
fieldNote: She chooses **new cash saving** over equipment spending because the shop lacks signed orders.
Her **current school costs** do not persist automatically into 2036, when both children are adults.

steps.text: Keep morning depot calls before releasing driver routes
Save two hundred only after full salary, collected shop pay, mortgage paid, no large school cost
Apply for posted role if post-2036 depot work lacks authority or bill-paying wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because scheduling posts could go before drivers have a real way to override a wrong route. Written severance, a dispatcher with authority and enough paid time to learn floor decisions would help. Our savings are a cushion. An unfinished tailoring order is not a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask a driver where the van actually waited when the map said the bay was clear. The map called it the shortest route, but the driver still had to turn the van. I would rather hear that driver than praise a perfect travel-time score.

headlineQuote: An unfinished tailoring order is not a wage.
portrait: **Sara, 43**, is an MBA-trained senior scheduling manager for a large parcel company.
Her **higher salary**, tailor husband, nine-month reserve and many nearby offices support a mortgage and two children.
She uses **AI occasionally** to check routes, but depot radio and driver reports decide what reaches a roster.
She is **calm** with mild change and anxious about possible loss of her well-paid scheduling post.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her scheduling post before drivers receive an effective override.
whatWouldHelp: Written **severance**, route authority and paid supervised depot work would help.
